module.title: Decorators & Generators
module.subtitle: Wrapping functions with @decorators and pausing execution with yield
lesson_points: Functions are objects in memory, so one function can wrap another function to add logging, timing, or checks (@decorator).
Writing '@log_call' above 'def greet():' is shorthand for 'greet = log_call(greet)'.
A generator uses 'yield' instead of 'return'—pausing its stack frame and handing back one value at a time until asked for the next.

quizzes.title: Stepping a Generator
quizzes.prompt: What does the second next(gen) call print?
quizzes.code:
def steps():
    yield "first"
    yield "second"

gen = steps()
_ = next(gen)
print(next(gen))
quizzes.explanation: The first next(gen) pauses at yield 'first'; the second next(gen) resumes right after it and yields 'second'.

quizzes.title: Spot the Broken Decorator Wrapper
quizzes.prompt: Click the line in wrapper() that throws away the wrapped function's return value.
quizzes.explanation: Line 3 calls fn(x) without 'return fn(x)', so wrapper returns None instead of 6.

quizzes.title: Why Use yield Instead of Building a List?
quizzes.prompt: What is the main memory advantage of yielding items one by one in a generator?
quizzes.sample_explanation: A generator produces one item at a time on demand instead of allocating a giant list holding millions of items in memory all at once.
quizzes.explanation: Lazy evaluation keeps memory usage tiny when processing large streams or files.
